newsitem.title: UK: IRA bomb victim dies, fuelling N.Ireland tension.
newsitem.headline: IRA bomb victim dies, fuelling N.Ireland tension.

text.p: A British soldier caught in the first IRA bombing in Northern Ireland for over two years died of his injuries on Friday, bringing down fresh condemnation on the republican guerrillas and their political allies.

Artificer Sergeant-Major James Bradwell, 43, was the first British soldier to die on active duty in Northern Ireland since the Irish Republican Army (IRA) and its Protestant Loyalist rivals called ceasefires in 1994.
The father-of-three was one of 31 people injured in the double car bombing at the British Army's headquarters in Northern Ireland at Lisburn, 10 miles (15 km) from Belfast.

British Prime Minister John Major said the bombing had only damaged the IRA's chances of getting its political wing, Sinn Fein, into multi-party peace talks and launched an emotional attack on Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams.
"Don't tell me this has nothing to do with you. I don't believe you, Mr Adams, I don't believe you," Major said in his keynote speech to the annual Conservative Party conference.
"He (Bradwell) was murdered in cold blood in the United Kingdom. I sent him there, Mr Adams, so spare me any crocodile tears," added Major.
Sinn Fein has been barred from joining the talks, sponsored by Britain and Ireland, until the IRA renews a 17 month truce it ditched in February with bombs in mainland Britiain.
Gerry Adams said Britain's failure to have a "good faith engagement" had brought a three year peace process to collapse.
"Political leaders and armed groups must take responsibility for their actions and the consequences of those actions," he said in a statement.
"I have never shirked mine. Mr Major cannot evade his responsibility and he must bear the lion's share of blame for the current difficulties."
Adams extended sympathy to the families of the soldier and and a 12-years-old Catholic boy accidentally killed by a vehicle in an altercation in Portadown south of Belfast on Tuesday.
They were "personal tragedies for their families and a sad reminder of the effect of conflict," he said.
Earlier Irish Prime Minister John Bruton, who this week accused the IRA of using Nazi tactics, said violence would not help the republicans' campaign for a united Ireland.

Bradwell's death came as the IRA's pro-British Loyalist rivals contemplated their response to the Lisburn bombing, which some fear will lead them to abandoning their own ceasefire and reigniting Northern Ireland's quarter-century of sectarian war.
Some Loyalist political leaders said Bradwell's death could make it more likely the guerrillas would resort to violence.

"It is obviously a tragedy and likely to have a negative response from Loyalists...This is the sort of action that could actually plummet us back into the depths of war, " said Billy Hutchinson, of the Progressive Unionist Party, the political arm of the outlawed Ulster Volunteer Force.
"I still insist that Loyalists should remain calm and hold on to the ceasefire," he told Reuters.

The Combined Loyalist Command, which rules over the Protestant guerrilla groups, is expected to meet soon and newspapers said it might issue a statement on Sunday, the second anniversary of its ceasefire.
The IRA is fighting to end British rule in Northern Ireland.
